NoteTexAccessor::command_names¶

Back to Note TeX Accessor API Reference

Signature¶

TokenBatch NoteTexAccessor::command_names() const

Extract TeX Control-Word Names¶

command_names() scans each cell for TeX control words and returns their names without the leading backslash. A control word begins with \ followed by ASCII letters or @; the letter/@ run is the name, and an immediately following * is retained. Thus \alpha, \section*, and \foo@bar yield alpha, section*, and foo@bar.

Control symbols are a different TeX form and are deliberately absent. Escaped specials such as \$ and \% do not have word names. The linebreak command \\ is consumed as a control symbol, so letters immediately following it are not falsely reported as a command. This distinction matters when extracting features from mixed prose and layout source.

The method reports lexical occurrences, not a set. Names retain source order and duplicates remain duplicated. It does not determine whether a command is defined, distinguish built-ins from user macros, expand declarations, or discard comments. Apply strip_comments() first when commented source must not contribute names; use macro_use() when a deduplicated macro-oriented inventory is the intended result.

The return is a closed TokenBatch. Flat Text tokens() holds the names and Int64 offsets() maps every flattened source cell to a half-open token range. Undefined yields undefined tokens with offsets [0]; empty/plain-text cells produce empty ranges. Text is required, and extraction allocates only the matched names and offsets after one linear scan of the source bytes.

Example 1: Words, Stars, Internal Names, Symbols, And Linebreaks¶

const auto source = pluss::make_note({
    R"(\alpha + \section*{Intro} + \foo@bar)",
    R"(line break: \\alpha; symbols: \$ and \%; then \beta)",
    "plain text"});
const auto names = source.tex().command_names();

std::cout << names.tokens() << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["alpha", "section*", "foo@bar", "beta"]

alpha after the linebreak \\ is plain following text, while the later \beta is a control word.

Example 2: Offsets Preserve Source Cells¶

std::cout << "offsets=[";
const auto offsets = names.offsets().integers();
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < offsets.size(); ++i)
  std::cout << (i ? ", " : "") << offsets[i];
std::cout << "]\n";

Output¶

offsets=[0, 3, 4, 4]

Example 3: Undefined Produces The Closed Empty Sentinel¶

const auto absent = pluss::Note::undefined().tex().command_names();
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "undefined names="
          << absent.tokens().defined() << " offsets=["
          << absent.offsets().integers()[0] << "]\n";

Output¶

undefined names=false offsets=[0]

Example 4: Native Integer Cells Reject¶

try {
  (void)pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::int64_t>{1, 2})
      .tex().command_names();
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "command names Int64: rejected\n";
}

Output¶

command names Int64: rejected
